title: First Flight
summary: A persona-led, route-spanning orientation that teaches contributors how to find current evidence, follow the architecture, and stop safely when the portal exposes planned intent.

personas.label: New contributor
personas.summary: Build a safe mental model before touching application code.
personas.outcome: You can identify the owning surface, distinguish evidence from intent, run the basic repository commands, and prepare a small change safely.

stops.title: Read truth before instructions
stops.instruction: Inspect lifecycle status, verification date, and provenance before trusting a procedure.
stops.why: The portal distinguishes current implementation from ratified target intent.

stops.title: Map the four surfaces
stops.instruction: Locate the storefront, admin, API, and developer portal responsibilities.
stops.why: A correct first change begins by identifying which application owns the behavior.

stops.title: Follow dependencies inward
stops.instruction: Trace UI and edge concerns toward ports and the core domain.
stops.why: The dependency rule is the fastest test for whether a proposed change belongs in the right layer.

stops.title: Interpret lifecycle labels
stops.instruction: Learn why implemented, scaffolded, planned, deferred, and deprecated are evidence labels rather than percentages.
stops.why: A polished page is not proof that its described runtime behavior exists.

stops.title: Learn the safe command surface
stops.instruction: Identify the package-manager, workspace, build, test, and portal commands used by this repository.
stops.why: Using the repository's own entry points avoids hidden environment and dependency drift.

stops.title: Close with evidence
stops.instruction: Use the documentation pull-request checklist to prepare a reviewable handoff.
stops.why: A change is easier to trust when code, docs, verification, and known gaps move together.

personas.label: Frontend developer
personas.summary: Trace a customer or operator interaction through Angular routing, state, data, and verification.
personas.outcome: You can choose the correct frontend surface, state owner, server-data boundary, and definition-of-done checks for a change.

stops.title: Start from the current frontend reality
stops.instruction: Review which state and data paths are working, transitional, fixture-backed, or unwired.
stops.why: Current behavior must remain visibly separate from the target frontend architecture.

stops.title: Orient inside the storefront
stops.instruction: Map a public experience from the file-based page into feature and data-access layers.
stops.why: Pages should stay thin while reusable behavior remains in the appropriate feature boundary.

stops.title: Trace filename to URL
stops.instruction: Follow the Analog file-based routing convention before adding or moving a customer route.
stops.why: Route ownership determines rendering, data loading, and browser-only safety.

stops.title: Choose the state owner
stops.instruction: Use the decision table to distinguish server state, complex client mutation, and local feature state.
stops.why: TanStack Query, classic NgRx, and SignalStore solve different ownership problems.

stops.title: Compare the operator surface
stops.instruction: Review how admin routes, feature families, and services differ from the public storefront.
stops.why: Storefront and admin share contracts and conventions, but they do not share every interaction or state boundary.

stops.title: Prove the frontend change
stops.instruction: Close the flight with architecture, behavior, rendering, interaction, and verification checks.
stops.why: Responsive visuals alone do not prove loading, failure, keyboard, SSR, or contract behavior.

personas.label: Backend developer
personas.summary: Trace a request from its validated contract through the domain ports, adapters, persistence evidence, and decision gates.
personas.outcome: You can place a backend change at the correct boundary and identify the runtime, schema, and decision evidence required to call it complete.

stops.title: Lock the dependency direction
stops.instruction: Read the controller-to-port-to-use-case-to-adapter flow before opening implementation files.
stops.why: Provider and persistence concerns must remain replaceable at the edges.

stops.title: Map the backend platform
stops.instruction: Identify the six architectural boundaries and the responsibilities between them.
stops.why: The atlas provides the shared vocabulary used by request, contract, domain, and persistence documentation.

stops.title: Separate the four shapes
stops.instruction: Distinguish transport contracts, domain types, persistence models, and response serialization.
stops.why: Shape leakage is a common way to accidentally couple the core to an adapter.

stops.title: Read the port boundary
stops.instruction: Check what the core may depend on and how edge capabilities are expressed as ports.
stops.why: A swappable edge begins with a stable inward-facing contract.

stops.title: Trace a real request
stops.instruction: Follow the current request path and compare it with the ratified target before proposing missing stages.
stops.why: The request trace exposes which boundaries are real today and which remain planned.

stops.title: Inspect persistence evidence
stops.instruction: Use the constellation to distinguish 37 graph-backed current nodes from 30 target ghosts and the separate 40-model source catalogue.
stops.why: An architecture plan does not make a collection implemented.

stops.title: Check governed decision gates
stops.instruction: Inspect unresolved decisions and their blast radius before crossing a blocked seam.
stops.why: A technically plausible default must not silently replace an unresolved product or architecture decision.

personas.label: Platform operator
personas.summary: Move from verified readiness boundaries through configuration, health evidence, local persistence, and recovery entry points.
personas.outcome: You can distinguish a successful build from operational readiness and identify the evidence required before running or documenting a production procedure.

stops.title: Start with the current scope
stops.instruction: Identify which runbooks define ratified structure and which procedures have been exercised.
stops.why: Planned operations content is not production evidence.

stops.title: Map environment and services
stops.instruction: Review local configuration, Docker Mongo replica-set assumptions, and browser runtime config.
stops.why: Local parity depends on starting the same supporting boundaries the applications expect.

stops.title: Separate secrets from public config
stops.instruction: Trace server-only secrets and deploy-time browser configuration through their approved injection paths.
stops.why: Browser bundles must never receive server credentials or provider secrets.

stops.title: Inventory operational reality
stops.instruction: Separate existing workflow and infrastructure artifacts from the remaining deployment work.
stops.why: A repository file can establish intent without proving a running environment.

stops.title: Read the target health contract
stops.instruction: Distinguish liveness from dependency readiness and the evidence each signal must carry.
stops.why: A responsive process can still be unable to serve real traffic.

stops.title: Verify the local Mongo lifecycle
stops.instruction: Review the single-node replica-set lifecycle and the evidence available from the current adapter.
stops.why: Transaction-capable topology and application connectivity require separate checks.

stops.title: Enter recovery through symptoms
stops.instruction: Use the troubleshooting map to move from an observed symptom toward the relevant evidence and runbook.
stops.why: Recovery should begin with scoped evidence, not speculative configuration changes.
